title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about writing with argument, structure and sources. You can already treat writing as a process and get a draft down. The next step is shaping that draft into an argument. By the end you will be able to structure an argumentative essay, integrate academic sources so they support your argument, and give your writing a critical edge.

These are not abstract study skills. Most of your marks come from written argument, in every subject. Shaping a case, using sources well, and showing your criticality are what lift a competent draft into strong academic work.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: structure an argumentative essay so that its introduction, body and conclusion carry one argument
integrate academic sources into a paragraph so they support your own argument
give your writing a critical edge by engaging actively with sources and signalling your criticality.

title: In real academic practice
body: Written argument is how most of your learning is judged. Every essay that asks you to assess, discuss or evaluate wants a position held together across paragraphs and supported by sources you have weighed. Build these habits now and they carry into every module of your degree, and into the reasoned, well-evidenced writing that professional work later asks of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, the argumentative essay: how structure carries an argument from introduction to conclusion. Second, integrating academic sources: using the voices technique so sources support your argument. Third, developing a critical edge: engaging actively with what you read and signalling your criticality. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can structure an argumentative essay so that its introduction, body and conclusion carry one argument.
I can integrate academic sources into a paragraph so they support my own argument.
I can give my writing a critical edge by engaging actively with sources and signalling my criticality.

title: Orientation
body: You can already get a draft down. The next step is making that draft do something: carry an argument. At university the most common genre is the argumentative essay, a piece built around a single, reasoned response to a question. This lesson looks at what that genre is and how its structure carries the argument for you.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are past treating writing as simply getting words on the page. At this level you are expected to shape those words into a case. You are not yet writing to the fine conventions of your own discipline, which comes later. The aim here is to build and sustain one argument across a whole essay.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe the argumentative essay as a continuous response built around a single argument
recognise how an argument is carried by an essay's introduction, body and conclusion in a worked example
identify what a strong introduction must do when you start an essay in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
An essay is a continuous piece of writing that sets out a response, usually as an argument, to a question or task. The kind you meet most often is the argumentative essay: a case shaped by your reading of the relevant discourse and supported by evidence. Writing agility, the ability to write well across the genres different assessments ask for, is itself a mark of strong academic work.

The argument is carried by structure. An essay needs a beginning, a middle and an end: an introduction, a body and a conclusion. The argument does not sit in one place; it emerges from how the parts are arranged, each paragraph making one point that moves the case forward.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of an essay you wrote recently. Did it carry one clear argument from start to finish, or was it more a set of separate points? What is one thing you could change in the introduction to state your line of argument sooner?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: The argumentative essay is a continuous response built around one argument, and that argument is carried by structure. The introduction sets up the topic and states the line of argument; the body makes one point per paragraph and orders those points so the case builds; the conclusion synthesises them without repeating. You can now recognise the argument in each part and say what a strong introduction must do. The next lesson shows how sources are woven in to support it.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw how an essay's structure carries its argument. This lesson is about the material you build that argument from: academic sources. The difference between a strong writer and a weaker one is not how many sources they cite, but what they do with them. Here you learn to make sources work for your argument.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are expected to do more than find relevant sources and report them. At this level, sources should serve your case, not stand in for it. You are not yet judged on the conventions of your own discipline. The aim here is to put your own voice first and let sources support it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: distinguish using a source to support your argument from merely reporting what it says
give an example of weaving several sources into one paragraph using the voices technique
choose where to place your own voice when integrating a source in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Integrating sources means using them to support or enhance your argument, not reporting what they say. The weaker habit is to list findings one after another, so the paragraph reads as a summary of other people's work. The stronger habit puts your view first and brings sources in to back it, qualify it, or set up a contrast.

A reliable way to do this is the voices technique. Your own voice opens the paragraph with a clear statement of its point. You then bring in the voice of one source, perhaps a second that supports it, then a contrasting voice, before returning to your own voice with a short judgement. The sources are present, but the paragraph is yours.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Find a paragraph in something you wrote recently that uses sources. Does your own voice lead it, or does it read as a list of what others said? What is one change that would put your argument back in charge?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Integrating sources means using them to support your argument rather than reporting them. The voices technique keeps your own voice in charge: you state the point, bring in supporting and contrasting voices, then close with your own judgement. You can now tell using a source from reporting it, and arrange several voices in a single paragraph. The next lesson sharpens this into a critical edge.

title: Orientation
body: You can shape an argument and weave sources into it. This lesson is about the quality that marks out strong academic writing: a critical edge. Being critical is not a paragraph you add at the end; it starts the moment you open a source, and it shows in the way you write about what you have read.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are expected to engage with sources, not simply describe them. At this level, criticality should run through your writing rather than appear once. You are not yet held to the critical conventions of your own discipline. The aim here is to use sources actively and to signal your criticality so a reader can see it.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use sources actively to build your own argument rather than describe what you have read
tell writing with a critical edge apart from writing that only reports sources
match a phrase from the language of criticality to the critical move it signals in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A critical edge begins before you write. As you read, set each source against everything else you have read: link viewpoints, compare and contrast them, analyse the data in one, weigh the recommendations in another. The hard part is carrying that engagement into your writing so the reader can see it.

Two moves do most of the work. First, use sources actively: lead with your own argument and draw on sources to support and extend it, rather than describing what you read. Second, flag your criticality with the language of criticality. Words and phrases such as 'suggests', 'however' or 'this implies' act as beacons, signalling to the reader that you are weighing a source, not just repeating it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at a piece of writing where you used sources. Could a reader see where you were being critical, or did the sources simply get reported? Which one phrase from the language of criticality could you add to signal a judgement?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A critical edge starts as you read and shows in how you write. You use sources actively, leading with your own argument, and you signal your criticality with the language of criticality, so a reader can see each move you make. You can now tell critical writing from writing that only reports, and name the move a critical phrase signals. With structure, sources and a critical edge in place, your writing can carry a real argument.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Your writing can now carry an argument. You can structure an argumentative essay so its introduction, body and conclusion hold one case, with each paragraph making a single point that moves the argument forward. You can integrate sources using the voices technique, keeping your own voice in charge so sources support your argument rather than replace it. And you can give your writing a critical edge, using sources actively and signalling your judgements with the language of criticality. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, writing with argument is something you do in every module. Each essay you shape around one case, each paragraph where your own voice leads the sources, each judgement you signal rather than leave implied, is this course at work. It is also what professional life rewards: clear, reasoned, well-evidenced writing that takes a position and defends it travels well beyond your degree.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced academic writing course takes these skills into writing within your own discipline, where the conventions of your subject shape how you argue. Going wider: the same habits underpin Criticality, Referencing and Researching, where you put argument, sources and a critical edge to work on real tasks. If any part still feels new, the introductory course revisits the writing process and the basics.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 145 to 181 of Chapter 9, 'Writing for Assessment', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Explore the concept
body: An argumentative essay moves through four structural stages. Reveal each stage to see the work it does for your argument.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal what it does. Work through all four.

_items.title: Introduction
_items.body: Introduce the topic, nod to the relevant discourse, and state clearly what you will argue and why. By the end of the introduction the reader should know your line of argument.

_items.title: Body: one point per paragraph
_items.body: Each paragraph makes a single point. It opens with a topic sentence, develops the point with evidence, and closes by linking that point back to the argument.

_items.title: Body: ordering the points
_items.body: Arrange the paragraphs so the case builds. Put the strongest or most important point where it carries most weight. The order itself is part of the argument.

_items.title: Conclusion
_items.body: Synthesise the points into the argument without repeating them. Make your case as clear as you can, and look outward to what it means.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students write the introduction to an essay on the same question.

{{learner-a}} opens with two broad sentences about why the topic matters, then lists what the essay 'will look at'. It reads smoothly, but it never says what will be argued. The reader reaches the body with no sense of a position, so each paragraph arrives as a separate point rather than a step in a case. This is structure without an argument.

{{learner-b}} introduces the topic, notes briefly how the discourse tends to treat it, and ends with a clear line of argument: what will be argued, and why. Now the body has something to carry. Each paragraph can make one point that advances that argument, and the reader can follow the case building. This is structure doing its job.

Both introductions are well written. Only {{learner-b}} used the structure to set up an argument the rest of the essay could carry.

title: Structuring the argument
body: Use these checks on your next essay to make sure its structure carries one argument.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Does my introduction end with a clear statement of what I will argue?
Does each body paragraph make one point, opened by a topic sentence?
Does each paragraph link its point back to the argument?
Are the paragraphs ordered so the case builds rather than wanders?
Does my conclusion synthesise the points rather than repeat them?
If I read only the first sentence of each paragraph, can I still follow the argument?

title: Explore the concept
body: The voices technique arranges several voices in one paragraph, with yours in charge. Review each card to see the part it plays.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Information cards about the voices technique.

_items.title: Your voice, first
_items.subtitle: Opens the paragraph
_items.text: Begin with a clear statement of the paragraph's point, in your own words. This sets the direction, so the sources that follow serve your argument.

_items.title: A supporting voice
_items.subtitle: Backs the point
_items.text: Bring in a source that supports your point, and, if useful, a second that reinforces it. The sources are evidence for your case, not a summary of the field.

_items.title: A contrasting voice
_items.subtitle: Tests the point
_items.text: Introduce a source that complicates or challenges the point. A contrasting voice shows you have weighed the discourse rather than cherry-picked it.

_items.title: Your voice, again
_items.subtitle: Closes the paragraph
_items.text: Return to your own voice with a short judgement that weighs the voices you have heard. The paragraph ends where it began: with your argument.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students write a paragraph drawing on the same four sources.

{{learner-a}} writes: one source found a problem; another reported the same; a third noted a different issue; a fourth found things had improved. Each sentence reports a source, in the order they were read. The paragraph is accurate, but it has no point of its own. The reader learns what four authors said, not what {{learner-a}} makes of it. This is reporting.

{{learner-b}} opens in their own voice with the paragraph's point, then brings the sources in to serve it: a supporting voice, a second that reinforces it, then a contrasting voice that complicates the picture. The paragraph closes in {{learner-b}}'s voice with a short judgement that weighs them. The same four sources now support an argument. This is the voices technique.

Both students used the sources. Only {{learner-b}} kept their own voice in charge of the paragraph.

title: Using the voices technique
body: Use these checks on a paragraph that draws on sources.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Does my own voice open the paragraph with its point?
Is each source brought in to support, extend or contrast with my point?
Have I included a contrasting voice, not only voices that agree?
Does the paragraph close in my voice with a short judgement?
Could a reader state the paragraph's point without reading the citations?
Have I avoided simply listing findings in the order I read them?

title: Explore the concept
body: Read the paragraph and select each marked phrase to see the critical move it signals to the reader.
instruction: Select each highlighted phrase to reveal the move it signals.

_term.definition: A hedging word. It signals that you are treating a finding as provisional rather than settled, so the reader sees you weighing the claim, not just reporting it.
A contrast marker. It signals a turn in the argument: you are about to set a competing view or a limitation against what came before, showing you have weighed both.
An inference marker. It signals that you are drawing your own conclusion from the evidence, rather than leaving the reader to connect it, which is a critical move.

_passage.text: the claim is not yet secure. The stronger studies,

_term.definition: A comparison marker. It signals that you are setting sources against each other and evaluating their relative weight, rather than listing them side by side.
A concession marker. It signals that you are granting a point that could count against you, which shows the reader you have weighed the opposing case rather than ignored it.

_passage.text: , the newer trials are larger, and that strengthens their case. But

_term.definition: An emphasis marker. It signals which point you judge to carry the most weight, steering the reader to the step that matters most in your argument.

_passage.text: , they measure different outcomes, so the studies are not strictly comparable. A careful reader weighs that before drawing a conclusion.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students write about the same two studies.

{{learner-a}} writes: the first study found a positive effect, and the second study also found a positive effect. The sentence is true and the sources are there, but nothing signals a critical mind at work. The two studies simply sit next to each other. A reader cannot tell what {{learner-a}} makes of them, because no judgement has been voiced. This is reporting without a critical edge.

{{learner-b}} writes: the first study suggests a positive effect; however, its sample was small, which implies the result should be read with caution. The second study, by contrast, is larger and points the same way, so the case is stronger than either alone. Here the language of criticality does visible work. The reader can see each move: a hedge, a contrast, an inference, an evaluation. This is a critical edge.

Both students read the same studies. Only {{learner-b}} made their criticality visible on the page.

title: Sharpening the critical edge
body: Use these checks on a passage where you engage with sources.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: Did my critical reading begin as I read, by linking and comparing sources?
Does my own argument lead, with sources used to support it?
Have I used hedging words where a claim is provisional?
Have I used contrast markers where I set one view against another?
Have I signalled my own inferences and judgements, not just reported findings?
Could a reader point to the words that show where I am being critical?

title: Formative check: the argumentative essay
displayTitle: Which statement best describes an argumentative essay?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best describes an argumentative essay?

_items.text: A continuous response to a question, built around a single argument.
_items.feedback: Yes. The argumentative essay is one case, carried across the whole piece.

_items.text: A summary of everything the main sources say about the topic.
_items.feedback: That reports the sources; an argumentative essay makes a case of its own.

_items.text: A list of separate points, each interesting in its own right.
_items.feedback: Separate points are not yet an argument; the essay must hold one case.

_items.text: A personal opinion written without reference to any discourse.
_items.feedback: An argument is shaped by the discourse and supported by evidence, not opinion alone.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The argumentative essay is a continuous response built around one argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about a single argument carried through the whole piece.
_incorrect.final: An argumentative essay is a continuous response built around one argument. The others describe a summary, a list, or an unsupported opinion.

title: Formative check: structure carrying the argument
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second introduction stronger than the first?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second introduction stronger than the first?

_items.text: It ended with a clear line of argument, so the body had a case to carry.
_items.feedback: Yes. Stating the argument lets each paragraph advance it.

_items.text: It was longer and used more impressive vocabulary.
_items.feedback: Length and vocabulary were not the difference; a stated argument was.

_items.text: It listed everything the essay would look at.
_items.feedback: Listing topics is what the weaker introduction did; it stated no argument.

_items.text: It avoided mentioning the discourse around the topic.
_items.feedback: The stronger introduction nodded to the discourse; it did not avoid it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second introduction stated a line of argument the body could carry.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what let the body build a case rather than offer separate points.
_incorrect.final: The second introduction ended with a clear line of argument. The weaker one listed topics and stated no case.

title: Formative check: a strong introduction
displayTitle: You are starting an essay in {{context}}. Which introduction does what a strong introduction must?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which introduction does what a strong introduction must when starting an essay?

_items.text: One that introduces the topic, notes the discourse, and states what you will argue.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, a strong introduction ends by stating your line of argument.

_items.text: One that describes the topic broadly and promises to 'look at' several areas.
_items.feedback: Describing and promising to look at areas states no argument.

_items.text: One that saves your position for the conclusion to keep the reader guessing.
_items.feedback: Holding back your argument leaves the body with no case to carry.

_items.text: One that opens with a long quotation and little else.
_items.feedback: A quotation is not an argument; the introduction must state your line.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a strong introduction ends with a clear statement of what you will argue.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the introduction that states a line of argument, not one that only describes.
_incorrect.final: A strong introduction in {{context}} introduces the topic, notes the discourse, and states what you will argue. The others describe, delay or decorate.

title: Formative check: using versus reporting sources
displayTitle: Which of these shows a source being used to support an argument, rather than reported?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option shows a source used to support an argument rather than reported?

_items.text: Your point leads the sentence, and the source is brought in as evidence for it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Using a source means it serves your argument.

_items.text: Each sentence states what a different author found, one after another.
_items.feedback: That lists findings; it reports the sources rather than using them.

_items.text: The paragraph summarises the main source from beginning to end.
_items.feedback: A running summary reports a source; it does not use it for your case.

_items.text: The sources appear in the order you happened to read them.
_items.feedback: Reading order is not an argument; the sources are not serving a point.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A source is used when your point leads and the source supports it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where your argument leads and the source backs it.
_incorrect.final: Using a source means your point leads and the source serves it. Listing, summarising or ordering by reading all report instead.

title: Formative check: the voices technique
displayTitle: In the worked example, how did the second student weave the four sources into one paragraph?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How did the second student weave the four sources into one paragraph?

_items.text: Own voice first, then supporting and contrasting voices, then a closing judgement.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the voices technique, with the student's voice in charge.

_items.text: By reporting each source in turn in the order they were read.
_items.feedback: That is the weaker paragraph; it reports rather than weaves.

_items.text: By removing the contrasting source so the point looked stronger.
_items.feedback: A contrasting voice was kept; dropping it would weaken the critical case.

_items.text: By quoting all four sources at length with no comment.
_items.feedback: Long quotation without comment is not the voices technique.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student led in their own voice and arranged supporting and contrasting voices around it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where the student's voice frames the sources.
_incorrect.final: The second student opened in their own voice, brought in supporting and contrasting voices, and closed with a judgement. The others report, cut or quote.

title: Formative check: placing your own voice
displayTitle: You are integrating a source into a paragraph in {{context}}. Where should your own voice go?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Where should your own voice go when integrating a source?

_items.text: Leading the paragraph with its point, and returning at the end with a judgement.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, your voice frames the paragraph and the source serves it.

_items.text: Only in a footnote, so the sources carry the paragraph.
_items.feedback: If the sources carry it, the paragraph reports rather than argues.

_items.text: Nowhere; a paragraph of sources speaks for itself.
_items.feedback: Without your voice, the reader cannot tell what you make of the sources.

_items.text: At the very end only, after the sources have been listed.
_items.feedback: A voice only at the end leaves the body of the paragraph as a list.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, your voice leads the paragraph and returns with a judgement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option where your voice frames the paragraph, not one where sources carry it.
_incorrect.final: Your voice should lead the paragraph and return at the end. Hiding it, dropping it or saving it for last leaves the sources reporting themselves.

title: Formative check: using sources actively
displayTitle: What does it mean to give your writing a critical edge when you use sources?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to give your writing a critical edge when using sources?

_items.text: Leading with your own argument and weighing sources, signalling the moves you make.
_items.feedback: Yes. A critical edge means active use, made visible to the reader.

_items.text: Describing each source carefully and accurately in turn.
_items.feedback: Careful description is still reporting; it does not weigh the sources.

_items.text: Adding one critical paragraph at the end of the piece.
_items.feedback: Criticality runs throughout; it is not a bolt-on paragraph.

_items.text: Citing as many sources as possible to show wide reading.
_items.feedback: Quantity of sources is not a critical edge; what you do with them is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A critical edge means using sources actively and signalling each move.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about weighing sources and showing it, not describing or counting them.
_incorrect.final: A critical edge means leading with your argument, weighing sources, and signalling the moves. Describing, bolting on or counting sources is not it.

title: Formative check: critical edge versus reporting
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second passage critical where the first only reported?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second passage critical where the first only reported?

_items.text: It hedged, contrasted and drew an inference, so the reader could see judgements being made.
_items.feedback: Yes. The language of criticality made the thinking visible.

_items.text: It mentioned more studies than the first passage.
_items.feedback: The number of studies was not the difference; visible judgement was.

_items.text: It avoided taking any position on the studies.
_items.feedback: Avoiding a position is the opposite of a critical edge.

_items.text: It quoted the studies directly instead of summarising them.
_items.feedback: Direct quotation is not what gave the passage its critical edge.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second passage made its criticality visible through hedges, contrasts and an inference.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about visible judgement, not the number or form of the sources.
_incorrect.final: The second passage hedged, contrasted and inferred, so judgement was visible. The others change the count, form or stance, not the criticality.

title: Formative check: the language of criticality
displayTitle: You are writing in {{context}} and want to signal that a claim is provisional. Which phrase does that?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which phrase signals that a claim is provisional?

_items.text: 'The evidence suggests', which hedges the claim rather than asserting it.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, a hedge like 'suggests' marks a claim as provisional.

_items.text: 'It is a fact that', which states the claim as settled.
_items.feedback: That asserts the claim; it does not mark it as provisional.

_items.text: 'Obviously', which tells the reader not to question it.
_items.feedback: That closes down questioning rather than hedging the claim.

_items.text: 'Everyone knows that', which appeals to common opinion.
_items.feedback: An appeal to common opinion is not a hedge and weakens criticality.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a hedge such as 'the evidence suggests' marks a claim as provisional.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the phrase that softens a claim rather than asserting it as settled.
_incorrect.final: A hedge like 'the evidence suggests' marks a claim as provisional. The others assert, dismiss or appeal to opinion.

body: What is the defining feature of an argumentative essay?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the defining feature of an argumentative essay?

_items.text: It is built around a single argument, carried across the whole piece.
_items.feedback: Yes. One argument holds the essay together.

_items.text: It gathers as many sources as possible on the topic.
_items.feedback: Source count is not what defines an argumentative essay.

_items.text: It keeps each paragraph's point separate from the others.
_items.feedback: The points must serve one case, not stand apart.

_items.text: It states its position only in the conclusion.
_items.feedback: The argument should be set out in the introduction.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An argumentative essay is built around one argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what holds the whole essay together.

body: Where in an essay should the line of argument first be made clear?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Where should the line of argument first be made clear?

_items.text: At the end of the introduction.
_items.feedback: Yes. The introduction should end by stating what you will argue.

_items.text: Only in the final sentence of the conclusion.
_items.feedback: That leaves the body with no case to carry.

_items.text: Spread evenly so it never appears in one place.
_items.feedback: A reader needs the argument stated, not hidden.

_items.text: In a footnote, to keep the main text neutral.
_items.feedback: The argument belongs in the main text, in the introduction.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A strong introduction ends with the line of argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the body needs before it can build a case.

body: What does it mean to integrate a source rather than report it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to integrate a source rather than report it?

_items.text: To use the source to support your own argument.
_items.feedback: Yes. Integration means the source serves your case.

_items.text: To restate what the source says, accurately, in full.
_items.feedback: That is reporting, not integrating.

_items.text: To place sources in the order you read them.
_items.feedback: Reading order does not integrate a source into an argument.

_items.text: To quote the source at length without comment.
_items.feedback: Unexamined quotation is not integration.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Integrating a source means using it to support your argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whose argument the source is serving.

body: In the voices technique, where does your own voice belong in a paragraph?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Where does your own voice belong in a paragraph using the voices technique?

_items.text: Leading the paragraph and returning at the end with a judgement.
_items.feedback: Yes. Your voice frames the paragraph.

_items.text: Only after every source has been reported.
_items.feedback: That leaves the body of the paragraph as a list.

_items.text: Removed entirely, so the sources speak for themselves.
_items.feedback: Without your voice, the paragraph cannot carry your argument.

_items.text: In a single hedge word at the very start.
_items.feedback: Your voice must state the point, not just hedge.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Your voice leads the paragraph and returns with a judgement.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about who should be in charge of the paragraph.

body: What gives a piece of writing a critical edge?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What gives a piece of writing a critical edge?

_items.text: Using sources actively and signalling your judgements to the reader.
_items.feedback: Yes. A critical edge is active use made visible.

_items.text: Describing each source thoroughly and in turn.
_items.feedback: Thorough description is still reporting.

_items.text: Adding one critical paragraph at the end.
_items.feedback: Criticality should run throughout.

_items.text: Citing more sources than anyone else.
_items.feedback: A critical edge is not about the number of sources.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A critical edge is using sources actively and showing your judgements.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the reader should be able to see on the page.

body: Which phrase is a beacon from the language of criticality that signals a contrast?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which phrase signals a contrast in the language of criticality?

_items.text: 'However'.
_items.feedback: Yes. 'However' marks a turn to a competing view or a limitation.

_items.text: 'For example'.
_items.feedback: That introduces an illustration, not a contrast.

_items.text: 'In addition'.
_items.feedback: That adds a similar point; it does not contrast.

_items.text: 'As stated above'.
_items.feedback: That refers back; it does not mark a contrast.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'However' signals a contrast.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the phrase that turns the argument to a competing view.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: how structure carries an argument, how to integrate sources so they support that argument, and how to give your writing a critical edge. On their own they are three separate moves. This lesson brings them together into one way of writing.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to write a flawless essay. The aim is to see structure, sources and a critical edge as one practice rather than three separate ideas, so that your own argument leads every piece you write from here on.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect structure, source integration and a critical edge into one argument-led way of writing
analyse how structure, source use and a critical edge work as one in a worked example of argument-led writing
apply the three together to keep your own argument in charge when you write about {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body: Argument-led writing is strong academic writing seen as one practice. Your own argument is always in charge. Structure carries it from introduction to conclusion, integrated sources support it, and a critical edge shows your judgement of those sources. The three moves from the earlier lessons are parts of that one practice.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this is what you do in almost every piece of writing you are set. You decide the one argument, then let structure, sources and a critical edge carry it, rather than treating them as separate boxes to tick. The more you write this way, the more it becomes how you write, not an extra step.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of writing you have coming up. What is the one argument you want it to make, and how will you keep structure, sources and your critical edge all serving that argument?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Strong academic writing is one practice, not three separate skills. You decide your argument, then let structure carry it, sources support it, and a critical edge show your judgement. It is keeping that argument in charge, across every piece you write, that lifts your work.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following sources.

_items.title: See pages 42 to 43 of Chapter 3 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 73 to 74 of Chapter 5 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The steps as one process
body: Argument-led writing comes together as a sequence. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Decide argument
_items.body: Decide the one argument your whole piece will make in answer to the question.

_items.title: Plan structure
_items.body: Plan a structure where each paragraph makes one point that moves that argument forward.

_items.title: Integrate sources
_items.body: In each paragraph, lead in your own voice and bring in sources to support your point.

_items.title: Sharpen the edge
_items.body: Sharpen the critical edge, signalling your judgements so the reader can see your argument at work.

title: Worked example
body: Two students answer the same essay question. One writes a clear structure, but reports sources in turn and adds a critical comment at the end, so the parts never quite join up. The other decides the argument first, then lets structure, sources and a critical edge all serve it, and the essay reads as one case. The second student wrote with their argument in charge.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep your argument in charge
body: Use these checks on any piece of writing to keep your own argument leading, with structure, sources and a critical edge serving it.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Does my whole piece make one clear argument in answer to the question?
Does my structure carry that argument, with one point per paragraph?
Does my own voice lead each paragraph, with sources brought in to support it?
Have I signalled my criticality, so the reader can see my judgements?
If I removed the citations, would my argument still stand on its own?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat structure, sources and a critical edge as one practice rather than three separate techniques?
body: Why is it more useful to treat structure, sources and a critical edge as one practice rather than three separate techniques?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat structure, sources and a critical edge as one practice rather than three separate techniques?

_items.text: Because they serve one argument together: structure carries it, sources support it, and a critical edge shows your judgement of them.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three moves are parts of one practice, held together by the argument they all serve.

_items.text: Because using all three at once means you never have to plan your essay.
_items.feedback: Planning the argument comes first. The three moves serve that plan, they do not replace it.

_items.text: Because learning one technique well is enough to write a strong essay for good.
_items.feedback: No single move is enough on its own. Strong writing needs the three working together.

_items.text: Because treating them separately takes less thought than using them together.
_items.feedback: The point is not less thought. It is that one argument should lead all three moves at once.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Structure, sources and a critical edge are three parts of one practice, all serving the argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what holds the three moves together: the one argument they all serve.

displayTitle: A student plans one argument, structures the essay so each paragraph moves it forward, leads paragraphs in their own voice with sources, and signals their judgements. What does this show?
body: A student plans one argument, structures the essay so each paragraph moves it forward, leads paragraphs in their own voice with sources, and signals their judgements. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student plans one argument, structures the essay so each paragraph moves it forward, leads paragraphs in their own voice with sources, and signals their judgements. What does this show?

_items.text: Argument-led writing at work: structure, sources and a critical edge all serving one argument.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three moves are working together as one practice, with the argument in charge.

_items.text: That the student used too many sources and should cut some out.
_items.feedback: The number of sources is not the point. The point is that they all serve one argument.

_items.text: That structure alone was enough to make the essay strong.
_items.feedback: Structure is one part. Here it works with integrated sources and a critical edge.

_items.text: That the critical edge was added at the end, separate from the rest.
_items.feedback: The critical edge ran through the writing, not tacked on. It is part of one practice.

_feedback.correct: That's right. This is the three moves working as one practice, with the student's argument in charge.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how structure, sources and the critical edge all serve the one argument.

displayTitle: You want to use argument-led writing to write better about {{context}} this term. Which plan best keeps your own argument in charge?
body: You want to use argument-led writing to write better about {{context}} this term. Which plan best keeps your own argument in charge?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use argument-led writing to write better about your subject this term. Which plan best keeps your own argument in charge?

_items.text: Decide your argument first, build a structure that carries it, lead each paragraph in your own voice with sources, and signal your judgements.
_items.feedback: Yes. The argument leads, and structure, sources and a critical edge all serve it.

_items.text: Gather as many sources as you can and report each one in turn, in the order you read them.
_items.feedback: That reports sources rather than using them. Your own argument should lead, not the sources.

_items.text: Write the structure, sources and critical comments as three separate drafts, then staple them together.
_items.feedback: They are one practice, not three drafts. The argument should hold all three together from the start.

_items.text: Add a critical paragraph at the very end, once the sources have all been described.
_items.feedback: A critical edge runs through the writing. It is not a paragraph added at the end.

_feedback.correct: That's right. When your argument leads, structure, sources and a critical edge all pull the same way.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The best plan keeps your own argument in charge of all three moves.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What does it mean to write with your argument in charge?
body: What does it mean to write with your argument in charge?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to write with your argument in charge?

_items.text: Your one argument leads, and structure, sources and a critical edge all work together to serve it.
_items.feedback: Yes. One argument leads, and the three moves serve it.

_items.text: You cite the greatest possible number of sources to show how much you have read.
_items.feedback: The number of sources is not the point. They should serve your argument.

_items.text: You keep structure, source use and criticality as three separate tasks done one after another.
_items.feedback: They are one practice, not three separate tasks.

_items.text: You save your own view for the conclusion and report sources everywhere else.
_items.feedback: Your voice should lead throughout, not wait until the conclusion.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A paragraph opens with the writer's point, brings in a supporting source and a contrasting one, signals a judgement with 'however', and moves the essay's argument forward. Which best describes it?
body: A paragraph opens with the writer's point, brings in a supporting source and a contrasting one, signals a judgement with 'however', and moves the essay's argument forward. Which best describes it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A paragraph opens with the writer's point, brings in a supporting source and a contrasting one, signals a judgement with 'however', and moves the essay's argument forward. Which best describes it?

_items.text: Argument-led writing, with structure, sources and a critical edge all serving one argument.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three moves are working together, led by the argument.

_items.text: Reporting, because it lists what several sources say in turn.
_items.feedback: The writer's voice leads and weighs the sources, so this is not reporting.

_items.text: A conclusion, because it brings the whole essay to an end.
_items.feedback: This is one paragraph doing the work, not an essay's conclusion.

_items.text: A plan, because it sets out what the essay will later look at.
_items.feedback: This paragraph makes its case, rather than listing what is to come.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
